question: We're baselining a lunar habitat atmosphere at 30% O2 and 10.2 psi. Which microgravity tests in PSI come closest to those conditions, and do any of them actually match both at once?
expected_answer: None match both conditions in the same test. The closest is FLEX: 24 droplet tests ran at O2 >= 0.30 mole fraction, but at 10.33-14.91 psi; the nearest is test #37 (O2 0.34, ~10.33 psi), just above the 10.2 psi limit. The only FLEX test below 10.2 psi (~10.18 psi) used 0.18 O2. BASS-II, Saffire-I and Saffire-II all stayed at or below ~22% O2. The system should flag this as a data gap rather than report a 'match'.

question: Do we have any measured flammability data at lunar gravity that I could use to certify cabin fabrics for a Moon base?
expected_answer: No. PSI currently contains no partial-gravity combustion data. LUCI and FM2 are expected to add it; FM2 is described as the first combustion experiment on another planetary body (1/6 g). ACME's E-FIELD only mimics partial gravity with an electric field. Microgravity and 1-g results may bound intermediate gravity, but that is an inference, not a measurement.
notes: Correct behavior: state the gap, don't extrapolate as fact

question: Which PSI investigation tested the highest oxygen concentration in microgravity, and can I pull its data from our corpus?
expected_answer: ACME's CFI-G, with an O2/N2 mixture of up to 85% O2 issuing from a spherical burner (inside-out gas flame). This is stated in the challenge text, but no CFI-G documents or data are in our corpus, so detailed conditions can't be retrieved; also it is a gaseous-fuel flame, not a solid-material flammability test.

question: Saffire-II was meant to check flammability limits near 21% O2. Did the silicone samples sustain burning in microgravity, and how does that compare with the same samples in the 1-g test?
expected_answer: In microgravity all four silicone samples (0.27-1.03 mm) had insignificant burning (~0 burn length). In 1-g, 2-1 burned completely with acceleratory spread, 2-2 burned 7.6 cm at 1.2 mm/s, 2-3 ~0, and 2-4 (opposed) completely at 0.6 mm/s. So for silicone near 21-22% O2, the 1-g test was the more severe case. SIBAL fabric, by contrast, burned the full 29 cm in microgravity (2-5: 145 s, 2.1 mm/s).
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017

question: For a large cotton-fiberglass panel in a spacecraft-like ventilation flow, how much does flow direction matter for how far and how fast fire spreads?
expected_answer: In Saffire-I (20 cm/s, ~21.5% O2), the concurrent burn (I-1) ran ~420 s over ~84 cm at ~1.8 mm/s, while the opposed burn (I-2) ran ~70 s over ~10 cm at ~1.3 mm/s. Saffire-III (25 cm/s) showed the same pattern: concurrent ~84 cm at 2.3 mm/s vs opposed ~10 cm at 0.98 mm/s. Concurrent (with-the-flow) spread is the dominant hazard.
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017
notes: Only 1-2 tests per condition; answer should note small n

question: We're writing ISS fire response procedures. Is aiming an extinguisher at the base of the flame, as we'd train on Earth, the right guidance in microgravity?
expected_answer: Not necessarily. On Earth the base of the flame is the stabilization point and where fresh air enters, so it is the usual target. In microgravity the best application point may not be obvious, especially for obstructed or wake-stabilized flames, and the suppressant stream can entrain O2 and strengthen the flame. BASS observed nitrogen applied to a flame strengthening it, and found local suppressant application inadequate: the jet entrained air and sustained the flame even with ambient flow off.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)

question: What does FLEX tell us about whether terrestrial inert-gas suppressant design margins carry over to spacecraft?
expected_answer: They don't fully. FLEX found that flammability limits are lower in reduced gravity, so terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants don't offer the same safety margin in low gravity. FLEX aimed for the most conservative estimate of the limiting oxygen index (LOI) for steady combustion.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)

question: Which diluents were tested in FLEX, and across what ranges of O2, CO2 and helium does the experiment table span?
expected_answer: Heptane and methanol droplets in O2/N2 diluted with a second inert gas (N2, CO2, He, or Xe per the ISS guide; the PSI record also mentions SF6 as a target suppressant). The FLEX table (274 tests: 157 methanol, 117 heptane) spans O2 0.12-0.34, CO2 0-0.70 and He 0-0.45 mole fraction.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)
notes: Sources list slightly different suppressant sets

question: Why can't we just reuse terrestrial smoke detector designs on a spacecraft, and which experiments addressed this?
expected_answer: Smoke properties from fires depend on buoyancy, so microgravity smoke differs, and spacecraft need rapid detection with few false alarms. DAFT measured background aerosol levels on ISS (using a modified P-Trak); SAME measured the particle-size distribution of smoke from spacecraft materials. One SAME instrument was reused in DAFT to detect dust.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)
notes: Corpus has no SAME/DAFT data; answer from overview sources only

question: We're running a crewed ground test in a pressurized, high-O2 cabin. Which Apollo 1 findings should drive our test safety review?
expected_answer: Pure O2 made the fire spread fast; rising temperature and pressure ruptured the CM pressure vessel and toxic gases killed the crew (burns likely survivable). The ignition source was never pinned down (arcing found in wiring near the environmental control system). The three-piece hatch took 90 s to open under ideal conditions and couldn't be opened under pressure. The test was classed non-hazardous because the rocket was unfueled, so safety organizations didn't review it and there was no rescue/treatment process. Fixes: 3-second unified hatch, restricted combustibles, fire-resistant suits.

question: What happened in the 1997 Mir fire, and what changed operationally afterwards?
expected_answer: A solid-fuel oxygen generator (lithium perchlorate canister) in Kvant-1 ignited, producing a ~3 ft flame, molten metal and dense smoke that blocked the path to one Soyuz. Six crew donned masks; extinguisher foam limited damage and the flame eventually went out on its own; life support cleared smoke over hours. Likely cause: latex glove material contaminating the canister. Afterwards Russia changed emergency training, ground controller response and canister ground preparation; ISS now relies on redundant electrolysis O2 systems with SFOG as backup.
expected_sources: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA, 2022)
unmapped_sources: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA, 2022)

question: The Apollo 13 tank failure wasn't a cabin fire. What design-change lesson is still relevant to oxygen systems on a lunar habitat?
expected_answer: Heater voltage was raised from 28 to 65 V DC without updating the thermostatic switches; heaters left on during a pad test hit ~1000 °F and degraded the Teflon wiring insulation in the O2 tank. Lesson: verify every dependent component when a design parameter changes. Redesign added a third tank in a separate bay, upgraded thermostats, removed stirring fans, and sheathed wiring in stainless steel; the board also recommended reviewing all cryogenic-O2 systems.

question: Compare the Apollo 1 and Mir fires: oxygen as a factor, ignition, and why one crew survived.
expected_answer: Both involved oxygen: Apollo 1 had a 100% O2 cabin; at Mir the fire came from an O2-generating canister. Apollo 1's ignition source was never identified (wire arcing suspected); Mir's likely cause was contamination in the canister. Apollo 1's crew couldn't escape (hatch couldn't open under pressure) and died of toxic gases; Mir's crew had masks and extinguishers, contained it, and life support removed the smoke.
expected_sources: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA, 2022)
unmapped_sources: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA, 2022)

question: The FLEX PSI description says LOI tests were run at 0.5-1.5 atm, but the experiment table goes up to ~3 atm. Which range should I trust?
expected_answer: Both are in the sources, and the FLEX detailed-results report reconciles them: tests ran at 0.70-3.05 atm (most between 0.7 and 1 atm, many in air), with the maximum capped near 3 atm by a conservative safety analysis of the CIR chamber (rated to ~9 atm). The table's 2319.9 mmHg (~3.05 atm) is therefore real. The 0.5-1.5 atm text describes the planned LOI procedure. One table row has 0 mmHg and should be treated as missing.
expected_sources: Detailed Results From FLEX, NASA/TP-2015-216046 (Dietrich et al., 2015)

question: What flow speeds were actually used in Saffire-II? The sources don't seem to agree.
expected_answer: Three versions exist: the PSI description says 20 or 30 cm/s depending on material; the PSI experiment table lists 20 cm/s for all nine samples (and leaves sample 2-6's material blank); the Urban et al. 2017 results table lists 2-6 as cotton-fiberglass at 25 cm/s and the rest at 20 cm/s. The system should show all three with sources. Note also that Saffire-II O2 values were derived from measured CO2 production (table Note 1).
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017

question: Can I use the BASS-II 'fan display' / 'air display' columns as airflow velocity in cm/s?
expected_answer: No. They are raw instrument settings, not velocities. Converting them needs the fan calibration data (a separate PSI reference file); without it the airflow in cm/s should be reported as unknown.

question: What cabin pressure were the BASS-II tests run at?
expected_answer: Not available in the experiment table (no pressure column). The answer should say the value is not in the retrieved data and point to the BASS-II summary report as the place to check, rather than assume ISS standard pressure.

question: Saffire-III repeated the Saffire-I panel at a higher flow. What spread rates were measured, and how did they scale with flow?
expected_answer: Saffire-III (25 cm/s, ~21.2-21.0% O2): concurrent burn ~84 cm at 2.3 mm/s over ~300 s; opposed burn ~10 cm at 0.98 mm/s over ~60 s. Compared with Saffire-I at 20 cm/s (1.8 mm/s concurrent), concurrent spread was faster; the presentation notes the burn-time ratio (400 s vs 320 s) equals the inverse ratio of flame speeds, i.e. flame speed scales with air flow.
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017
notes: PSI-100 itself has only metadata in our corpus; results come from the paper

question: Can PSI microgravity combustion data inform fire risk inside a lander's rocket engine or propellant feed system?
expected_answer: Out of scope. Rocket and propellant fire safety is generally beyond PSI's research coverage: the high velocities in rocket engines make the combustion effectively independent of gravity.

question: What concrete firefighting equipment on Earth traces back to NASA spacecraft and spacesuit work?
expected_answer: Lightweight firefighter air tanks (with JSC and Scott Aviation): 20 lb for 30 min of air, 13 lb lighter, 4,500 psi, aluminum liner wrapped in resin-impregnated glass fiber. Project FIRES (NASA, FEMA's US Fire Administration, Marshall-managed): Apollo-derived fire-resistant, heat-protective materials for turnout gear, field-tested with 14 fire departments. The Shuttle-derived incipient fire detector, and water-mist extinguishers from ISS work.
expected_sources: NASA Spinoff: New Technology for the Fire Attire (1982)

question: Contrary to old speculation, how long did candle flames last on Mir, and what did that show about microgravity flammability?
expected_answer: Some microgravity candle flames burned for over 45 minutes before running out of fuel. Despite a much lower burning rate (nearly invisible), they burned down to a lower ambient O2 mole fraction than an identical candle on Earth.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)

question: On a thin fuel ignited mid-sample in low-speed flow, which way does the flame spread in microgravity versus 1-g?
expected_answer: In microgravity at low forced-flow speeds, it spreads upstream into the oncoming flow. In 1-g it always spreads downstream with the buoyant flow, even without forced flow.
expected_sources: A Researcher's Guide to: Combustion Science (ISS, 2015)

question: For sizing a microgravity fire model, what heat release rates and stoichiometry did the BASS-II small-sample fires produce?
expected_answer: Heat release rates were computed from O2 consumption and burn time using 13.1 kJ per gram of O2 consumed; most tests were well below 100 W. The global equivalence ratio averaged about 1.3 (fuel rich), from mass loss and O2 consumption. Before/after O2 and CO2 readings matched one-step gas-phase stoichiometry well; CO vs CO2 was linear for some datasets but not all geometries.
expected_sources: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: How did BASS-II get sub-ambient O2 inside the glovebox, and how long did it take to set up a low-O2 test?
expected_answer: The MSG working volume (0.25 m3) was diluted with ISS gaseous N2, the first time this was done on ISS. A continuously stirred tank reactor model set the N2 flow time and rate; the CSA-CP O2 reading was offset daily against the Major Constituents Analyzer. Dilution typically took 1-3 hours, with O2 taken from ~21% down to ~14% for near-limit flames.
expected_sources: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: Are melting plastics a particular spread hazard in microgravity? Is there any direct observation?
expected_answer: Yes. In a BASS-II wax candle test in opposed flow, the wick ejected a wax droplet directly upstream. The report notes this typifies the hazard of melting plastics in microgravity: if melt viscosity is low enough, burning droplets can be ejected and ignite other materials.
expected_sources: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: How many BASS-II tests were actually run against plan, and what were the main variables?
expected_answer: 126 tests versus 103 planned, because some samples were burned more than once. Main variables: ambient O2 concentration, ventilation flow velocity, and fuel type, thickness and geometry (PMMA rods 6.35-12.7 mm, slabs 0.125-5 mm, a 4 cm spherical section, cotton-fiberglass fabric).
expected_sources: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: What was the maximum airflow the BASS-II duct could deliver?
expected_answer: Sources differ: the PSI investigation record says up to 40 cm/s; the BASS-II summary report says ~55 cm/s with no flow restrictors and ~35 cm/s with two restrictors. The system should report both with sources.
expected_sources: BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: How big was the Saffire-I fire in power terms, and how does that compare with typical BASS-II glovebox fires?
expected_answer: Saffire-I (40.6 x 94 cm SIBAL, 20 cm/s concurrent) averaged ~1.8 mm/s spread with an estimated average flame power of 1200 +/- 300 W. Most BASS-II tests were well below 100 W, roughly an order of magnitude smaller.
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017
BASS-II Summary Report, NASA/TM-20210011385 (Olson et al., 2021)

question: Why did Saffire go to meter-scale samples instead of relying on earlier low-g flame spread experiments?
expected_answer: Prior low-g experiments used samples no larger than about 10 cm, while a serious spacecraft fire could consume an order of magnitude more material. The ~0.94 m x 0.4 m Saffire-I/III panel is at least an order of magnitude larger in both dimensions than any prior low-g flame spread test.
expected_sources: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire), Ruff & Urban, 46th ICES 2016

question: How long did the Saffire-I and Saffire-III concurrent burns last?
expected_answer: Within the same 2017 presentation, the results table gives ~420 s (Saffire-I) and ~300 s (Saffire-III), while the image-sequence slide says Saffire-I burned 400 s and Saffire-III 320 s. The PSI Saffire-I table also gives 420 s. The system should show the discrepancy.
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017

question: In Saffire-II, what happened to the PMMA-plus-Nomex composite sample?
expected_answer: Sample 2-7 (0.85 mm PMMA and 0.37 mm Nomex, concurrent, 20 cm/s) burned ~140 s: the PMMA portion was completely consumed but the Nomex was not ignited.
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017

question: Why was it hard to pick Saffire-II flammability-limit samples, and what was the test actually trying to determine?
expected_answer: Cygnus O2 was ~21% (same as ISS at hatch close), so materials had to be near their normal-gravity or hypothesized low-gravity maximum oxygen concentration (MOC) at 21%, but most spacecraft-relevant materials don't have 1-g limits near 21%. The goal was mainly to see whether flames propagated or self-extinguished (cameras as primary diagnostic), emulating the NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 configuration with bottom ignition.
expected_sources: Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire), Ruff & Urban, 46th ICES 2016

question: Is anyone planning to test fire growth in the elevated-O2, reduced-pressure atmospheres we expect for exploration habitats?
expected_answer: Yes: the proposed Saffire-IV, V and VI objectives include characterizing fire growth in high-O2, low-pressure atmospheres, along with demonstrating fire monitoring and cleanup technologies and validating models of a fire's impact on vehicle habitability. Results of those flights are not in our corpus (one Saffire-IV modeling paper is).
expected_sources: Saffire: A Novel Approach to Study of Spacecraft Fire Safety Using Un-manned Spacecraft, Urban et al., ASGSR 2017
Operation and Development Status of the Spacecraft Fire Experiments (Saffire), Ruff & Urban, 46th ICES 2016

question: Is there any known data-quality issue in the early FLEX droplet results I should account for?
expected_answer: Yes. The conformal coating on the early deployment needles could dissolve or flake into the fuel, contaminating droplets. The report concludes burning-rate constants, flame size histories and radiative extinction diameters were minimally or not affected, but disruptive extinction of methanol (and possibly heptane) and a few distorted droplets were probably caused by the contaminant. New uncoated needles were flown afterwards.
expected_sources: Detailed Results From FLEX, NASA/TP-2015-216046 (Dietrich et al., 2015)

question: What extinction modes did FLEX observe, and how did the measured LOI compare with expectations?
expected_answer: Both radiative extinction (at higher dilutions) and diffusive extinction (at lower dilutions) occurred for both fuels, plus disruptive extinctions; heptane results also gave soot information. Observed LOI values appeared slightly lower than initially expected, consistent with reduced-gravity limits being less forgiving than terrestrial assumptions.
expected_sources: Detailed Results From FLEX, NASA/TP-2015-216046 (Dietrich et al., 2015)
